h1:
Ayutthaya Temples at Night
The Ruins Lit Up After Sunset
intro: By day, Ayutthaya is a UNESCO World Heritage town that's hot and crowded. But once the sun goes down, another side of it shows up. Several of the ancient sites switch on floodlights, turning old red brick into a backdrop people queue up to photograph in Thai costume. We've pulled together the real lighting hours, entry fees and the best spots to shoot.

blocks.html: If you only have an evening in Ayutthaya, the good news is that this is when the town looks its best. The dusty heat fades, the air cools, and several of the ruins light up their chedis and prangs so you can see details you'd miss in daylight. The one place lit every single night, and the real highlight, is Wat Chaiwatthanaram. The temples inside the island town, like Wat Phra Si Sanphet and Wat Mahathat, light up during the cool-season festival period. Let's go through them one by one.

blocks.text: Wat Chaiwatthanaram — the star that's lit every night

blocks.html: If you're picking just one place to see at night, this is it. Wat Chaiwatthanaram sits on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River, just outside the island town. Built in the reign of King Prasat Thong, its central Khmer-style prang is ringed by smaller chedis. When the warm orange lights come on against the deep blue sky just after sunset, people don't stop shooting. The Fine Arts Department opens it for evening visits every day, so you don't have to wait for a festival.

items: Lighting / opening hours — roughly 6.30–10pm nightly (ticket sales usually stop around 9pm)
Entry fee — 10 THB for Thais · 50 THB for foreigners
Best window — 6.30–7.30pm, during blue hour before it's fully dark, so you get both the blue sky and the temple lights in one frame
Parking — there's a lot in front of the temple; it fills fast on weekends, so allow a little time to walk in

blocks.title: Photo tip
blocks.html: Get there before dark, around 6pm, and wait for blue hour so you catch both the sky glow and the temple lights. Once it's pitch dark the sky goes flat black and your shots lose depth. The classic angle is standing in front of the central prang with the smaller chedis lined up in a row behind it.

blocks.text: Island-town temples that light up during the festival

blocks.html: Within the historical park in the centre of the island town, the Fine Arts Department lights up the major ruins during the night tourism festival (generally around November to February, mostly Friday to Sunday). The temples below are the ones that get lit. If you time it right, the whole island turns into an open-air museum after dark.

items.name: Wat Phra Si Sanphet
items.blurb: Three Sri Lankan-style chedis in a row inside the old royal palace grounds. Lit from below, the chedis cast long shadows that look great. It's one of the most popular photo spots on the island.

items.name: Wat Mahathat
items.blurb: Home to the famous Buddha head wrapped in tree roots. At night the surrounding prangs and chedis feel more solemn and mysterious than they do in the daytime.

items.name: Wat Ratchaburana
items.blurb: Its tall central prang stands out right across from Wat Mahathat — you can walk between the two. You can climb the prang during the day; at night you take in the lights from below.

items.name: Wat Phra Ram
items.blurb: Sits beside Bueng Phra Ram lake, with the water reflecting the lit prang. Great for reflection shots, and far less crowded than the first two temples.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.html: The island-town temples are lit only during the festival and on certain days, not every night like Chaiwatthanaram. The dates shift year to year, so check the Ayutthaya Historical Park page or TAT before you go so you're not disappointed.

blocks.text: Renting a Thai costume — how it works and what it costs

blocks.html: Part of the charm of Ayutthaya at night is dressing up in period Thai costume for photos against the ruins. Around Wat Chaiwatthanaram there's a whole row of rental shops; you can just walk up and pick one on the spot. You don't need to book ahead on a weekday, but on long weekends it gets busy, so reserve in advance.

items: Costume rental — roughly 200–300 THB per person; many shops let you keep it all day at that price
Hair / makeup — add-ons run about 50 THB each; some shops include hair styling in the package
For men, women and kids — go for lighter tones, which contrast nicely with the red brick and orange lights
Nice extras — some shops lend umbrellas for free and help suggest photo angles; it's worth asking

blocks.html: An honest heads-up: the prices above are rough ranges from traveller reviews. Shops charge differently and adjust by season, so confirm the all-in price before you pay — costume, hair, and deposit — so there are no surprises when you return the outfit.

blocks.text: Making the most of a single evening

blocks.html: If you've only got one evening, focus on Chaiwatthanaram since it's open every night and it's the prettiest. Give yourself enough time there, then swing by the island-town temples if your visit lines up with the festival.

items: 4.30–5.30pm — arrive at a costume shop near Wat Chaiwatthanaram, pick an outfit and do your hair
6–6.30pm — enter the temple and wait for blue hour, shooting while the sky's still bright
7–8.30pm — catch the lit-up angles once it's dark and walk around the prang
After 8.30pm — return the costume and grab dinner around one of the night markets in town

blocks.title: Come prepared
blocks.html: Bring mosquito repellent — the riverside gets buggy in the evening. Wear shoes you can walk on brick and grass in. And if you're shooting on your phone, turn on Night mode to capture the lights with a lot more detail.

faq.q: What time does Wat Chaiwatthanaram light up?
faq.a: It's open for evening visits roughly 6.30–10pm every day, with ticket sales usually stopping around 9pm. The best window for photos is around 6.30–7.30pm, during blue hour before it's fully dark, when you can get both the sky glow and the temple lights in one frame.

faq.q: How much is entry to Ayutthaya's temples at night?
faq.a: Wat Chaiwatthanaram is 10 THB for Thais and 50 THB for foreigners. The temples in the historical park in the centre of the island town charge separate fees per temple, at similar prices. During some festival periods entry may be free, so it's worth checking before you go.

faq.q: Are the island-town temples lit every day?
faq.a: No. Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Wat Mahathat, Wat Ratchaburana and Wat Phra Ram are lit during the night tourism festival, generally around November to February and mostly Friday to Sunday — unlike Wat Chaiwatthanaram, which is lit every night. The dates change year to year, so check the Historical Park page or TAT first.

faq.q: How much does it cost to rent a Thai costume in Ayutthaya?
faq.a: Costume rental is roughly 200–300 THB per person, and many shops let you keep it all day. Hair and makeup add-ons run about 50 THB each. The shops are around Wat Chaiwatthanaram, so you can walk up and choose on the spot, but on long weekends it's best to book ahead — and confirm the all-in price, including the deposit, before you pay.

faq.q: Can I photograph the temples at night with a phone?
faq.a: Easily. Turn on Night mode and hold steady for 2–3 seconds to capture the lights and the texture of the brick. A small phone tripod helps a lot for sharper shots, especially for the water-reflection angle at Wat Phra Ram.
